To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in the general adult population of Finland has increased by about 50% during the last two decades, 2) the prevalence of metabolic syndrome in Finland is higher in men than in women, 3) the prevalence of MetS is higher in the middle-aged population, and 4) the prevalence of diabetes is about 50% higher in the subjects with MetS than in the non-metabolic syndrome subjects.

(i) the MetS, defined by the IDF criteria, is associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes; (ii) the association of the MetS with type 2 diabetes was stronger than the association with cardiovascular disease, but the risk of type 1 diabetes was not increased; (iii) the association between the MetS and type 2 diabetes did not differ by gender; (iv) the MetS is a stronger predictor of type 2 than of type 1di
• MetS is associated with an excess of mortality, especially from CVD.

we have shown that the metabolic syndrome is a heterogeneous entity with different pathogenetic mechanisms.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic syndrome is not a useful clinical concept.

there is no evidence that the metabolic syndrome predicts cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes, but that the presence of atherothrombosis is an independent predictor of cardiovascular outcomes.
the metabolic syndrome is not a disease but a risk factor, and it should be treated as such.
